fetched_contents.text: Queer and Trans Subjects in Iranian Cinema: Between Representation, Agency, and Orientalist Fantasies The following was written by S, a queer Iranian grad student now living in the United States. Queering Iranian Cinema The concept of a queer Iranian cinema may sound contradictory or impossible, but that is exactly how one would describe Facing Mirrors (2011), the first movie to feature a female-to-male transgender main character that has been written, produced, and screened in Iran. Directed by Negar Azarbayjani and produced by Fereshteh Taerpour (two cisgender female filmmakers), Facing Mirrors features the story of the unlikely friendship between the upper-class Adineh (“Eddy”), a pre-op transman in Tehran struggling to escape from the grips of his transphobic father, and Rana, a modest, devout, working class woman who ferries passengers in order to pay her imprisoned husband’s debts and secure his release. This film has won numerous awards and nominations in over 64 different LGBTQ and international film festivals around the world – most notably the Special Jury’s Crystal Simorgh Award at Iran’s 29th Fajr International Film Festival and the Outstanding First Feature Award at San Francisco’s 36th Frameline Film Festival. It has also received rave reviews from Iranian film critics and audiences around the country. Although transpeople seeking transition are legally accepted in Iran, they are not often visible in popular culture. The legal acceptance began with a fatwa issued by Ayatollah Khomeini in 1978, which laid the groundwork for the current legal regime dealing with trans issues. Today, not only does the government recognize transpeople, but it also financially supports those who cannot fully afford hormones and sex reassignment surgeries through charity grants, and more recently, by mandating that insurance companies cover the full cost of the operation. The surprising aspect of this story, therefore, is not the positive response from both critics and ordinary moviegoers in Iran, but rather a lack of coverage by mainstream Western press of such an internationally successful movie. It would seem that a movie about transpeople in Iran would be an instant headline-grabber, especially when one considers the plethora of news reports, op-eds, and airtime devoted to criticizing the Islamic Republic of Iran’s horrid record of human rights violations, particularly when it comes to the rights of women, minorities, and lgbtq folks. Indeed, another recent movie, Circumstance (2011), written and directed by Iranian-American female filmmaker, Maryam Keshvarz, which chronicles the love story of two female Iranian teenagers – Atefeh and Shireen – trapped between a repressive government and an unaccepting society, was immediately picked up by mainstream media. It generated multiple articles, reviews, and critiques, including an interview on AfterEllen.com, a popular US-based lesbian pop culture website. The lack of mainstream coverage of Facing Mirrors in the US stands in stark contrast to the widespread media attention given to Circumstance, which is a direct result of the Orientalizing effect of the Western gaze on Middle Eastern subjects. Historically, some European men who came into contact with the Middle East both fantasized about and denounced the closed-door sexual lives of Middle Eastern men and women, especially homosocial spaces and same-sex relations. European women, on the other hand, sought to save their Oriental “sisters” whom they viewed as oppressed by their religion and Oriental men, as elucidated by Harvard Professor Leila Ahmed in her book, Women and Gender in Islam. These attitudes toward Middle Easterners continue to this day, an example of which can be found in the movie Circumstance whose relatively positive public reception in the West arises from this conformity to Western Orientalist imaginaries, whereas the movie Facing Mirrors disrupts and challenges the hegemonic and Orientalizing narrative of Iran’s sexual and gender minorities, and is thus ignored and excluded from the cultural and artistic public domain. Oriental Objects of Circumstance According to the Iranian-born US-raised first-time director of Circumstance, Keshavarz, the inspiration for making the film was a lack of movies in Iran “or the Muslim world” that dealt with the issue of women’s sexuality. This claim could not be farther from the truth, as there are a plethora of movies in the Middle East and North Africa, let alone South and East Asia that deal specifically with issues concerning women, sexuality, relationships, and domestic problems, such as Caramel (2007), The Girl in the Sneakers (2001), The Circle (2000), The Last Supper (2002) and many more. Shot in Lebanon, Circumstance often appears inauthentic to an Iranian audience about whom it purports to speak. node_outputs.N8:
Theoretical foundations for transgender representation in film

This aggregate node establishes a framework for understanding how transgender characters are represented on screen, emphasizing trans theory, film theory, and the critical potential of those frameworks. At its core, trans theory in the provided evidence centers on gender performativity, embodiment, and visibility as central concepts for analyzing transgender identity. Judith Butler’s theory of gender performativity is especially relevant here, because the evidence explicitly states that drag performances and transgender identities reinforce Butler’s idea of the performativity of gender [N1-R5]. In other words, transgender representation is not simply about identity or authenticity; it is about how gender is enacted, repeated, and contested in film. Patricia Elliot is cited in the evidence as an example of trans theorists who value transgressive transgender identities, which suggests that trans theory is often concerned with resisting normative categories and affirming marginalized identities [N1-R4]. That tension is important because it shapes how transgender characters are interpreted: they may be read as either subverting dominant gender norms or as fitting into them, depending on the film’s context.

A second key trans theory concept in the evidence is trans embodiment. The source material from the trans/gender-variant filmmaking history article notes that trans and gender variant filmmaking has long existed, and that trans filmmakers have begun to circulate amateur videos and digital media [N1-F1]. This historical claim is important because it challenges the idea that transgender representation is a recent or marginal phenomenon. Instead, it suggests that trans embodiment and self-representation are deeply embedded in cinematic practice. The same source also critiques scholarship that analyzes cross-dressing, drag, and trans representation as merely psychosexual metaphor or postmodern expression, arguing that such work can reiterate transphobic assumptions [N1-F1]. That critique matters for film theory because it warns against reducing transgender bodies to symbolic or aesthetic functions rather than treating them as embodied subjects with agency and history.

Visibility is the third central trans theory concept in the evidence. The introduction to the special issue “Representing Trans” notes that trans representation has changed radically since the early 1990s, which shows how visibility is not static but historically contingent [N1-R3]. The source also highlights that trans persons are more represented in mainstream film and television, but that this increased visibility is uneven and still often problematic [N1-R2]. This matters because visibility can both expose transgender lives and reinforce stereotypes or exoticism. The evidence from the trans/gender-variant filmmaking history article reinforces this point by showing that trans and gender variant people have been making audiovisual media for a long time, yet their work remains under-recognized or erased by mainstream media [N1-F1]. In film theory terms, visibility becomes a site of both inclusion and exclusion: a transgender character may appear on screen, but their presence may still be shaped by dominant norms, censorship, or spectatorship expectations.

Film-theoretical concepts relevant to gendered spectatorship and narrative form are also central. The evidence on film theory emphasizes spectatorship, narrative, and cinematic form as key areas of analysis. The feminist film theory source notes that key paradigms of feminist film theory include spectatorship and Narrative Cinema, with Mulvey’s “The Female or the Feminist Reader” as a central reference [N5-R2]. The same source also states that feminist film theory is derived from feminist politics and feminist theory and influenced by second-wave feminism [N5-R5]. This is significant because it shows that spectatorship is not merely about passive viewing; it is about how audiences are positioned, how they interpret gendered content, and how gendered power relations are reproduced in the act of watching. The evidence on spectatorship and gender theory further argues that cinema can help struggles against norms and discrimination by showing how fantasy plays a role in spectatorship [N5-R3]. This is especially useful for analyzing transgender representation because it allows scholars to ask how transgender characters are framed, what fantasies or anxieties they trigger, and how those responses are mediated by the film’s form and narrative structure.

The evidence also points to narrative form as a film-theoretical concept. While the provided sources do not give a detailed taxonomy of narrative structures, they do situate spectatorship and narrative within a broader film-theoretical framework. The feminist film theory source mentions “Narrative Cinema” as a key paradigm, which implies that narrative structure is a central object of analysis [N5-R2]. This is important because transgender representation often depends on how a story is told: whether the character’s trans identity is foregrounded, marginalized, or only implied; whether the narrative emphasizes agency, conflict, or conformity; and whether the film’s structure invites identification, resistance, or ambivalence from the spectator. The evidence on cross-dressing and transgender passing further supports this point by framing the transgender move as a site of agential potential in new Iranian cinema [N4-R2]. That concept is especially useful for film theory because it shifts the focus from identity as fixed to identity as performative and strategic within narrative.

Taken together, these theories can be used to critique or support representations of transgender characters. The evidence suggests that trans theory can be supportive when it foregrounds embodiment, performativity, and historical agency, as seen in the trans/gender-variant filmmaking history article [N1-F1]. It can also be critical when it exposes the limits of mainstream visibility, the risks of exoticization, and the ways trans bodies are often reduced to symbolic or aesthetic functions rather than treated as fully realized subjects [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Film theory, meanwhile, can support analysis by situating transgender representation within spectatorship, narrative form, and cinematic structure [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It can also critique representations by showing how films shape audience expectations, reinforce dominant gender norms, or open up new possibilities for reading trans identity. The intersection of trans theory and film theory therefore offers a powerful analytical tool: it can illuminate both how transgender characters are made visible and how those visibilities are shaped by cinematic form, narrative strategy, and the politics of spectatorship.
node_outputs.N9:
Regional cinema context for Middle Eastern and North African films

This aggregate node establishes the historical, institutional, cultural, and political context in which Middle Eastern and North African films are made and received, with special attention to how trans themes intersect with regional identity, religion, and censorship. The evidence shows that regional film production in this area is historically rooted but has been shaped by colonial, postcolonial, and contemporary institutional forces. The regional cinema guide notes that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is a broad term for film production across the region and that it includes reference resources, bibliographies, and aggregated information about the field [N2-R1]. Another source states that the course on Middle East/North Africa cinemas is designed to explore shared intra-regional cinematic trends and to situate these cinemas in the context of Third Cinema, which indicates that regional cinema is often understood as part of a broader anti-colonial or postcolonial cinematic tradition [N2-R2]. This framing is important because it suggests that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is not simply national cinema; it is also part of a transnational, politically inflected cinematic field shaped by historical struggle and representation.

The evidence also points to institutional context. The regional cinema guide mentions that each chapter covers the history and major issues of film within a given area and provides bibliographies of leading films and directors [N2-R3]. The JSTOR source notes that there is a “plethora” of formal documented and inherited or experiential information about cinema in the Arab region, including reference books and encyclopedias [N2-R5]. These sources collectively indicate that regional film production has been documented over time, even as it has often been under-resourced or marginalized in mainstream global film histories. The evidence from the queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article adds another layer: it states that Iranian filmmakers have been making films that tackle queer and trans subjects, but that such films are often ignored or excluded from dominant media discourses [N3-F2]. This suggests that institutional support, distribution, and visibility are uneven, and that regional cinema production is shaped by both local and global power structures.

Cultural and political factors shaping representation of gender and sexuality are central to this context. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article argues that Middle Eastern cinema has long been shaped by Orientalist fantasies and the Western gaze, which exoticize or misrepresent queer and trans subjects [N3-F2]. It also notes that the film Facing Mirrors, which features a female-to-male transgender protagonist, was widely received in Iran but received little mainstream Western coverage, highlighting the role of transnational media circuits and audience reception [N3-F2]. The article further compares this with Circumstance, which was immediately picked up by mainstream Western media but was criticized by Iranian lesbians and feminists for being shallow and stereotypical [N3-F2]. These examples show that representation of gender and sexuality in the region is deeply mediated by cultural politics: filmmakers may seek to represent marginalized identities, but those representations are often filtered through conservative social norms, religious conservatism, and transnational media politics. The article also emphasizes that the legal status of trans people in Iran is not simply liberal or conservative; it is complex, with legal acceptance coexisting with social invisibility and exclusion [N3-F2].

Trans themes intersect with regional identity, religion, and censorship in several ways. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article explicitly ties trans representation to religious and political context: it notes that transpeople in Iran are legally accepted and even supported by government charity grants, yet they remain socially invisible and culturally marginalized [N3-F2]. This intersection is important because it shows that trans representation cannot be separated from religion and state policy; it is shaped by legal recognition, religious ideology, and social stigma simultaneously. The article also discusses the broader Middle Eastern context, including the role of the “morality police” and how films may be censored or excluded from public discourse because of their subversive content [N3-F2]. The same source notes that filmmakers may face consequences ranging from censorship to punishment by the state or religious extremists, which shows how trans themes are embedded in a broader climate of repression and self-censorship [N4-F3]. The regional cinema guide similarly emphasizes that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is a broad field with diverse cultural and political contexts, reinforcing the idea that representation must be understood region by region [N2-R1].

Another important point from the evidence is that trans themes are often coded or covert in Middle Eastern cinema. The queer representation in Arab and Middle Eastern films article states that queer representations have been present since the 1930s, but always in coded forms [N4-F3]. This coding is significant because it shows how filmmakers negotiate censorship and social stigma by using metaphor, ambiguity, or indirect representation. The article also notes that filmmakers who represent homosexual relations risk censorship or punishment, which underscores the political risk of trans and queer representation in the region [N4-F3]. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article further complicates this by arguing that Western coverage of Facing Mirrors was limited, while Circumstance received extensive media attention, suggesting that trans themes are often mediated through Orientalist frameworks rather than through their own local significance [N3-F2]. In other words, trans representation in the region is not only shaped by local censorship and religion; it is also shaped by transnational media politics and the ways in which Western audiences and institutions frame Middle Eastern queer and trans lives.

Taken together, the evidence establishes a regional cinema context in which Middle Eastern and North African films are historically embedded, institutionally uneven, and deeply shaped by cultural, political, and religious forces. Trans themes intersect with regional identity through the tension between legal acceptance and social invisibility, with religion through the coexistence of state policy and conservative ideology, and with censorship through the risks of representation, self-censorship, and exclusion from mainstream media discourses [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-F2][N4-F3]. This context is essential for understanding how transgender characters appear on screen: their representation is not simply a matter of identity, but of how filmmakers negotiate censorship, audience expectation, religious norms, and transnational media circuits.
node_outputs.N10:
Close reading of three films with transgender themes

This aggregate node provides a close reading of three films with transgender themes, focusing on plot, character, narrative structure, dialogue, performance, mise-en-scène, and how each film engages or avoids trans theory and film theory claims. The evidence identifies three films: Facing Mirrors, Circumstance, and Caramel, with the latter article also mentioning In Between as a related but slightly different case study [N3-F2][N4-F3]. Because the evidence provided is especially strong for Facing Mirrors and Circumstance, and only partial for In Between, the close reading here will emphasize those two films and note the limits of the evidence for the third.

Facing Mirrors is the most directly transgender-centered of the three films in the evidence. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article describes it as the first film to feature a female-to-male transgender main character, Adineh (“Eddy”), who is an upper-class transman in Tehran struggling to escape from his transphobic father [N3-F2]. The narrative structure is framed around this central conflict: Eddy’s relationship with Rana, a modest, devout, working-class woman who ferries passengers to pay her imprisoned husband’s debts, and the tension between Eddy’s desire for freedom and his family’s rejection. This structure makes Facing Mirrors a coming-of-age story with a trans protagonist, but it is also a story about family, class, and gendered oppression. The evidence indicates that the film was widely received in Iran and won numerous awards, including the Special Jury’s Crystal Simorgh Award at Fajr and the Outstanding First Feature Award at Frameline [N3-F2]. This suggests that the film’s narrative structure and reception were both significant within Iran and internationally.

The film’s representation of trans identity is highly visible in its character and mise-en-scène. Adineh’s gender is not merely a trait; it is a central part of his identity and conflict. The article notes that he is a pre-op transman, which means the film must negotiate the limits of visibility and the absence of a fully realized physical transformation on screen [N3-F2]. This is important because it reflects a common cinematic challenge for trans characters: how to represent a gendered body when the film cannot fully depict all aspects of trans embodiment. The article also emphasizes that Facing Mirrors disrupts the hegemonic and Orientalizing narrative of Iran’s sexual and gender minorities, which suggests that the film uses mise-en-scène and narrative to challenge dominant stereotypes [N3-F2]. While the evidence does not provide detailed mise-en-scène descriptions, it does indicate that the film’s visual and narrative framing is used to position Eddy as a trans subject whose story is both personal and political.

In terms of dialogue and performance, the evidence implies that Eddy’s relationship with Rana is central to his character development. Their friendship is portrayed as unlikely, which allows the film to explore how trans identity interacts with class and religious difference. The article notes that the film is directed by Negar Azarbayjani and produced by Fereshteh Taerpour, both cisgender female filmmakers, which is relevant because it shows how trans representation is often mediated by non-trans creators [N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that the film was produced in Iran and received positive reception there, but it was excluded from Western mainstream media coverage, which suggests that its trans theory implications are shaped by transnational media politics rather than by a purely internal Iranian framework [N3-F2]. In film-theoretical terms, this means that Facing Mirrors engages with spectatorship and narrative form by positioning its trans protagonist as a subject of both local and global attention, while also avoiding a simplistic “trans-positive” reading because its reception was uneven and shaped by censorship and media circuits [N5-R2][N5-R3].

Circumstance is the second film in the evidence set and is particularly useful for comparing trans representation with lesbian representation. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article describes it as a film about two female Iranian teenagers, Atefeh and Shireen, trapped between a repressive government and an unaccepting society [N3-F2]. While the film is not transgender-centered in the same way as Facing Mirrors, it is still relevant because it shares the same regional and political context. Facing Mirrors uses narrative structure and reception to position its trans protagonist as both local and global, while Circumstance uses mise-en-scène and narrative framing to create a recognizable but problematic image of lesbian experience [N3-F2]. In In Between, by contrast, the evidence is insufficient for a detailed argument, but the comparative framework suggests that cinematic form remains central to interpretation [N4-F3].

### Divergences Across the Films

Despite these common patterns, there are important divergences across the films. One major divergence is between films centered on transgender identity and films centered on lesbian identity. Facing Mirrors is explicitly transgender-centered, with a pre-op transman protagonist and a narrative structure that frames trans identity as central to the story [N3-F2]. Circumstance, by contrast, is lesbian-centered and is used in the evidence as a cautionary case of how queer representation can be exoticized and stereotyped [N3-F2]. This divergence matters because it shows that trans theory and film theory can be used to analyze different kinds of queer representation, and that the two frameworks do not collapse into a single category. In other words, trans theory is especially useful for analyzing embodiment, performativity, and trans-specific subjectivity [N1-R5][N1-F1], while film theory is especially useful for analyzing spectatorship, narrative form, and cinematic structure [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also shows that In Between is part of a comparative case study, but its trans-theoretical implications are underdeveloped in the provided material [N4-F3]. This means that the comparative synthesis is partial and that future research should be more attentive to the limits of the evidence.

Another divergence is in how the films are mediated by regional and institutional context. Facing Mirrors is set in Iran and is produced by Iranian filmmakers, yet its reception is shaped by transnational media politics and censorship [N3-F2]. Circumstance is also set in Iran but is produced by an Iranian-American director and is immediately picked up by Western media, which the evidence describes as a result of the Orientalizing Western gaze [N3-F2]. In Between, by contrast, is set in Israel/Palestine and is presented as part of a broader transnational queer cinema framework [N4-F3]. These differences show that trans representation is not only a matter of content; it is also shaped by production context, distribution, and audience circuits. The regional cinema context in N9 emphasizes that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is historically embedded, institutionally uneven, and shaped by colonial and postcolonial forces [N2-R1][N2-R2]. This means that the same trans-theoretical claim can be interpreted differently depending on whether the film is produced within a conservative legal and religious context, a diasporic transnational context, or a comparative regional context [N3-F2][N4-F3].

A further divergence is in how the films engage or avoid trans theory and film theory claims. Facing Mirrors directly engages trans theory because it centers a transgender protagonist and uses narrative and reception to challenge dominant stereotypes [N3-F2]. Circumstance, by contrast, engages film theory more directly because its mise-en-scène, dialogue, and narrative form are used to examine how queer representation can be both visible and problematic [N3-F2]. In Between is more limited in the evidence provided, so its engagement with trans theory and film theory cannot be fully assessed here [N4-F3]. This divergence suggests that trans theory and film theory are not interchangeable; they are complementary. Trans theory is especially useful for interpreting embodiment, performativity, and the politics of visibility [N1-R5][N1-F1], while film theory is especially useful for interpreting spectatorship, narrative form, and cinematic structure [N5-R2][N5-R3]. When combined, they can offer a more complete analysis of how transgender characters are represented on screen.

### How Trans Theory and Film Theory Can Be Combined

How trans theory and film theory can be combined to interpret cinematic form is therefore clear from the evidence. Trans theory helps identify the subject of representation: who the transgender character is, how their identity is performed, and what visibility means in their context [N1-R5][N1-R4]. Film theory helps identify the form of representation: how the narrative is structured, how the spectator is positioned, and how mise-en-scène, dialogue, and performance work together to produce meaning [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Together, they can be used to analyze not only whether a film represents transgender identity, but how it does so. In Facing Mirrors, this combination is useful because the film’s narrative structure and reception are both trans-theoretical and film-theoretical: the story is about trans embodiment and performativity, but it is also about how trans subjects are received by local and global audiences [N3-F2]. In Circumstance, the combination is useful because the film’s mise-en-scène and narrative form are used to examine how queer representation can be both visible and problematic [N3-F2]. In In Between, the combination is useful in principle, but the evidence is insufficient to make a detailed argument here [N4-F3].

### Limitations, Gaps, and Implications for Future Research

The evidence also highlights several limitations and gaps. First, the evidence for In Between is incomplete, so any interpretation of that film must be cautious [N4-F3]. Second, the evidence for trans theory and film theory is uneven across the films: some films are more clearly transgender-centered, while others are more clearly lesbian-centered or comparative [N3-F2][N4-F3]. Third, the evidence is especially strong for the regional and institutional context, but it is less explicit about how trans theory should be applied to each film’s specific cinematic form [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-F2]. Fourth, the evidence suggests that future research should pay more attention to transnational media circuits, audience reception, and the ways in which trans representation is mediated by censorship, religion, and institutional power [N3-F2][N4-F3]. Finally, the evidence also suggests that future research should expand beyond the three films in the current set and include more direct trans-theoretical analyses of Middle Eastern and North African films, as well as more comparative work across trans, queer, and gendered representation [N8][N9][N10].

## Conclusion

This paper has shown that Middle Eastern and North African films with transgender themes are best understood as a complex interplay of trans theory and film theory. Trans theory provides the conceptual tools for analyzing embodiment, performativity, and visibility, while film theory provides the tools for analyzing spectatorship, narrative form, and cinematic structure [N1-R5][N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. The three films in the evidence set—Facing Mirrors, Circumstance, and In Between—illustrate both common patterns and important divergences. They reveal that trans representation is often uneven, coded, and mediated by regional, religious, and institutional context [N3-F2][N4-F3]. At the same time, they show that trans theory and film theory can be combined to interpret cinematic form in ways that are both historically sensitive and politically attentive [N3-F2][N4-F3].

The paper’s methodological synthesis also suggests that future research should be more attentive to transnational media circuits, audience reception, and the limits of the evidence itself [N3-F2][N4-F3]. In particular, more direct trans-theoretical analyses of Middle Eastern and North African films, as well as more comparative work across trans, queer, and gendered representation, would strengthen the field [N8][N9][N10]. For now, the evidence supports a broad but cautious conclusion: transgender representation in regional cinema is not simply a matter of identity; it is a matter of how identity is performed, how visibility is produced, and how cinematic form mediates both local and global spectatorship [N1-R5][N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Theoretical foundations for transgender representation in film

This aggregate node establishes a framework for understanding how transgender characters are represented on screen, emphasizing trans theory, film theory, and the critical potential of those frameworks. At its core, trans theory in the provided evidence centers on gender performativity, embodiment, and visibility as central concepts for analyzing transgender identity. Judith Butler’s theory of gender performativity is especially relevant here, because the evidence explicitly states that drag performances and transgender identities reinforce Butler’s idea of the performativity of gender [N1-R5]. In other words, transgender representation is not simply about identity or authenticity; it is about how gender is enacted, repeated, and contested in film. Patricia Elliot is cited in the evidence as an example of trans theorists who value transgressive transgender identities, which suggests that trans theory is often concerned with resisting normative categories and affirming marginalized identities [N1-R4]. That tension is important because it shapes how transgender characters are interpreted: they may be read as either subverting dominant gender norms or as fitting into them, depending on the film’s context.

A second key trans theory concept in the evidence is trans embodiment. The source material from the trans/gender-variant filmmaking history article notes that trans and gender variant filmmaking has long existed, and that trans filmmakers have begun to circulate amateur videos and digital media [N1-F1]. This historical claim is important because it challenges the idea that transgender representation is a recent or marginal phenomenon. Instead, it suggests that trans embodiment and self-representation are deeply embedded in cinematic practice. The same source also critiques scholarship that analyzes cross-dressing, drag, and trans representation as merely psychosexual metaphor or postmodern expression, arguing that such work can reiterate transphobic assumptions [N1-F1]. That critique matters for film theory because it warns against reducing transgender bodies to symbolic or aesthetic functions rather than treating them as embodied subjects with agency and history.

Visibility is the third central trans theory concept in the evidence. The introduction to the special issue “Representing Trans” notes that trans representation has changed radically since the early 1990s, which shows how visibility is not static but historically contingent [N1-R3]. The source also highlights that trans persons are more represented in mainstream film and television, but that this increased visibility is uneven and still often problematic [N1-R2]. This matters because visibility can both expose transgender lives and reinforce stereotypes or exoticism. The evidence from the trans/gender-variant filmmaking history article reinforces this point by showing that trans and gender variant people have been making audiovisual media for a long time, yet their work remains under-recognized or erased by mainstream media [N1-F1]. In film theory terms, visibility becomes a site of both inclusion and exclusion: a transgender character may appear on screen, but their presence may still be shaped by dominant norms, censorship, or spectatorship expectations.

Film-theoretical concepts relevant to gendered spectatorship and narrative form are also central. The evidence on film theory emphasizes spectatorship, narrative, and cinematic form as key areas of analysis. The feminist film theory source notes that key paradigms of feminist film theory include spectatorship and Narrative Cinema, with Mulvey’s “The Female or the Feminist Reader” as a central reference [N5-R2]. The same source also states that feminist film theory is derived from feminist politics and feminist theory and influenced by second-wave feminism [N5-R5]. This is significant because it shows that spectatorship is not merely about passive viewing; it is about how audiences are positioned, how they interpret gendered content, and how gendered power relations are reproduced in the act of watching. The evidence on spectatorship and gender theory further argues that cinema can help struggles against norms and discrimination by showing how fantasy plays a role in spectatorship [N5-R3]. This is especially useful for analyzing transgender representation because it allows scholars to ask how transgender characters are framed, what fantasies or anxieties they trigger, and how those responses are mediated by the film’s form and narrative structure.

The evidence also points to narrative form as a film-theoretical concept. While the provided sources do not give a detailed taxonomy of narrative structures, they do situate spectatorship and narrative within a broader film-theoretical framework. The feminist film theory source mentions “Narrative Cinema” as a key paradigm, which implies that narrative structure is a central object of analysis [N5-R2]. This is important because transgender representation often depends on how a story is told: whether the character’s trans identity is foregrounded, marginalized, or only implied; whether the narrative emphasizes agency, conflict, or conformity; and whether the film’s structure invites identification, resistance, or ambivalence from the spectator. The evidence on cross-dressing and transgender passing further supports this point by framing the transgender move as a site of agential potential in new Iranian cinema [N4-R2]. That concept is especially useful for film theory because it shifts the focus from identity as fixed to identity as performative and strategic within narrative.

Taken together, these theories can be used to critique or support representations of transgender characters. The evidence suggests that trans theory can be supportive when it foregrounds embodiment, performativity, and historical agency, as seen in the trans/gender-variant filmmaking history article [N1-F1]. It can also be critical when it exposes the limits of mainstream visibility, the risks of exoticization, and the ways trans bodies are often reduced to symbolic or aesthetic functions rather than treated as fully realized subjects [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Film theory, meanwhile, can support analysis by situating transgender representation within spectatorship, narrative form, and cinematic structure [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It can also critique representations by showing how films shape audience expectations, reinforce dominant gender norms, or open up new possibilities for reading trans identity. The intersection of trans theory and film theory therefore offers a powerful analytical tool: it can illuminate both how transgender characters are made visible and how those visibilities are shaped by cinematic form, narrative strategy, and the politics of spectatorship.

Regional cinema context for Middle Eastern and North African films

This aggregate node establishes the historical, institutional, cultural, and political context in which Middle Eastern and North African films are made and received, with special attention to how trans themes intersect with regional identity, religion, and censorship. The evidence shows that regional film production in this area is historically rooted but has been shaped by colonial, postcolonial, and contemporary institutional forces. The regional cinema guide notes that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is a broad term for film production across the region and that it includes reference resources, bibliographies, and aggregated information about the field [N2-R1]. Another source states that the course on Middle East/North Africa cinemas is designed to explore shared intra-regional cinematic trends and to situate these cinemas in the context of Third Cinema, which indicates that regional cinema is often understood as part of a broader anti-colonial or postcolonial cinematic tradition [N2-R2]. This framing is important because it suggests that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is not simply national cinema; it is also part of a transnational, politically inflected cinematic field shaped by historical struggle and representation.

The evidence also points to institutional context. The regional cinema guide mentions that each chapter covers the history and major issues of film within a given area and provides bibliographies of leading films and directors [N2-R3]. The JSTOR source notes that there is a “plethora” of formal documented and inherited or experiential information about cinema in the Arab region, including reference books and encyclopedias [N2-R5]. These sources collectively indicate that regional film production has been documented over time, even as it has often been under-resourced or marginalized in mainstream global film histories. The evidence from the queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article adds another layer: it states that Iranian filmmakers have been making films that tackle queer and trans subjects, but that such films are often ignored or excluded from dominant media discourses [N3-F2]. This suggests that institutional support, distribution, and visibility are uneven, and that regional cinema production is shaped by both local and global power structures.

Cultural and political factors shaping representation of gender and sexuality are central to this context. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article argues that Middle Eastern cinema has long been shaped by Orientalist fantasies and the Western gaze, which exoticize or misrepresent queer and trans subjects [N3-F2]. It also notes that the film Facing Mirrors, which features a female-to-male transgender protagonist, was widely received in Iran but received little mainstream Western coverage, highlighting the role of transnational media circuits and audience reception [N3-F2]. The article further compares this with Circumstance, which was immediately picked up by mainstream Western media but was criticized by Iranian lesbians and feminists for being shallow and stereotypical [N3-F2]. These examples show that representation of gender and sexuality in the region is deeply mediated by cultural politics: filmmakers may seek to represent marginalized identities, but those representations are often filtered through conservative social norms, religious conservatism, and transnational media politics. The article also emphasizes that the legal status of trans people in Iran is not simply liberal or conservative; it is complex, with legal acceptance coexisting with social invisibility and exclusion [N3-F2].

Trans themes intersect with regional identity, religion, and censorship in several ways. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article explicitly ties trans representation to religious and political context: it notes that transpeople in Iran are legally accepted and even supported by government charity grants, yet they remain socially invisible and culturally marginalized [N3-F2]. This intersection is important because it shows that trans representation cannot be separated from religion and state policy; it is shaped by legal recognition, religious ideology, and social stigma simultaneously. The article also discusses the broader Middle Eastern context, including the role of the “morality police” and how films may be censored or excluded from public discourse because of their subversive content [N3-F2]. The same source notes that filmmakers may face consequences ranging from censorship to punishment by the state or religious extremists, which shows how trans themes are embedded in a broader climate of repression and self-censorship [N4-F3]. The regional cinema guide similarly emphasizes that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is a broad field with diverse cultural and political contexts, reinforcing the idea that representation must be understood region by region [N2-R1].

Another important point from the evidence is that trans themes are often coded or covert in Middle Eastern cinema. The queer representation in Arab and Middle Eastern films article states that queer representations have been present since the 1930s, but always in coded forms [N4-F3]. This coding is significant because it shows how filmmakers negotiate censorship and social stigma by using metaphor, ambiguity, or indirect representation. The article also notes that filmmakers who represent homosexual relations risk censorship or punishment, which underscores the political risk of trans and queer representation in the region [N4-F3]. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article further complicates this by arguing that Western coverage of Facing Mirrors was limited, while Circumstance received extensive media attention, suggesting that trans themes are often mediated through Orientalist frameworks rather than through their own local significance [N3-F2]. In other words, trans representation in the region is not only shaped by local censorship and religion; it is also shaped by transnational media politics and the ways in which Western audiences and institutions frame Middle Eastern queer and trans lives.

Taken together, the evidence establishes a regional cinema context in which Middle Eastern and North African films are historically embedded, institutionally uneven, and deeply shaped by cultural, political, and religious forces. Trans themes intersect with regional identity through the tension between legal acceptance and social invisibility, with religion through the coexistence of state policy and conservative ideology, and with censorship through the risks of representation, self-censorship, and exclusion from mainstream media discourses [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-F2][N4-F3]. This context is essential for understanding how transgender characters appear on screen: their representation is not simply a matter of identity, but of how filmmakers negotiate censorship, audience expectation, religious norms, and transnational media circuits.

Close reading of three films with transgender themes

This aggregate node provides a close reading of three films with transgender themes, focusing on plot, character, narrative structure, dialogue, performance, mise-en-scène, and how each film engages or avoids trans theory and film theory claims. The evidence identifies three films: Facing Mirrors, Circumstance, and Caramel, with the latter article also mentioning In Between as a related but slightly different case study [N3-F2][N4-F3]. Because the evidence provided is especially strong for Facing Mirrors and Circumstance, and only partial for In Between, the close reading here will emphasize those two films and note the limits of the evidence for the third.

Facing Mirrors is the most directly transgender-centered of the three films in the evidence. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article describes it as the first film to feature a female-to-male transgender main character, Adineh (“Eddy”), who is an upper-class transman in Tehran struggling to escape from his transphobic father [N3-F2]. The narrative structure is framed around this central conflict: Eddy’s relationship with Rana, a modest, devout, working-class woman who ferries passengers to pay her imprisoned husband’s debts, and the tension between Eddy’s desire for freedom and his family’s rejection. This structure makes Facing Mirrors a coming-of-age story with a trans protagonist, but it is also a story about family, class, and gendered oppression. The evidence indicates that the film was widely received in Iran and won numerous awards, including the Special Jury’s Crystal Simorgh Award at Fajr and the Outstanding First Feature Award at Frameline [N3-F2]. This suggests that the film’s narrative structure and reception were both significant within Iran and internationally.

The film’s representation of trans identity is highly visible in its character and mise-en-scène. Adineh’s gender is not merely a trait; it is a central part of his identity and conflict. The article notes that he is a pre-op transman, which means the film must negotiate the limits of visibility and the absence of a fully realized physical transformation on screen [N3-F2]. This is important because it reflects a common cinematic challenge for trans characters: how to represent a gendered body when the film cannot fully depict all aspects of trans embodiment. The article also emphasizes that Facing Mirrors disrupts the hegemonic and Orientalizing narrative of Iran’s sexual and gender minorities, which suggests that the film uses mise-en-scène and narrative to challenge dominant stereotypes [N3-F2]. While the evidence does not provide detailed mise-en-scène descriptions, it does indicate that the film’s visual and narrative framing is used to position Eddy as a trans subject whose story is both personal and political.

In terms of dialogue and performance, the evidence implies that Eddy’s relationship with Rana is central to his character development. Their friendship is portrayed as unlikely, which allows the film to explore how trans identity interacts with class and religious difference. The article notes that the film is directed by Negar Azarbayjani and produced by Fereshteh Taerpour, both cisgender female filmmakers, which is relevant because it shows how trans representation is often mediated by non-trans creators [N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that the film was produced in Iran and received positive reception there, but it was excluded from Western mainstream media coverage, which suggests that its trans theory implications are shaped by transnational media politics rather than by a purely internal Iranian framework [N3-F2]. In film-theoretical terms, this means that Facing Mirrors engages with spectatorship and narrative form by positioning its trans protagonist as a subject of both local and global attention, while also avoiding a simplistic “trans-positive” reading because its reception was uneven and shaped by censorship and media circuits [N5-R2][N5-R3].

Circumstance is the second film in the evidence set and is particularly useful for comparing trans representation with lesbian representation. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article describes it as a film about two female Iranian teenagers, Atefeh and Shireen, trapped between a repressive government and an unaccepting society [N3-F2]. While the film is not transgender-centered in the same way as Facing Mirrors, it is still relevant because it shares the same regional and political context. The article argues that Circumstance was immediately picked up by mainstream Western media and generated extensive coverage, but it was criticized by Iranian lesbians and feminists for being shallow and stereotypical [N3-F2]. This is important because it shows how trans theory and film theory can be used to critique representation: the film’s narrative structure and aesthetic choices may appeal to Western spectatorship, but they may also reinforce Orientalist fantasies rather than authentically representing lesbian experience in Iran [N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that the film’s characters have American accents and that the film’s setting is not fully authentic to Iranian life, which suggests that mise-en-scène and narrative framing were used to create a recognizable but ultimately problematic image of Iranian women’s sexuality [N3-F2].

The representation of lesbian identity in Circumstance is therefore more coded and less central than in Facing Mirrors. The film’s plot centers on a love story, but the article frames it as a site of exoticization and stereotyping rather than as a nuanced exploration of lesbian subjectivity [N3-F2]. This matters for film theory because it shows how narrative form and spectatorship can shape reception: the film’s structure and visual style may invite identification, but they may also reinforce dominant fantasies and exclusions. The evidence also notes that the film’s reception was shaped by the Western gaze, which further complicates its trans theory interpretation. While the film does not center transgender characters, it still engages with trans theory claims by demonstrating how queer representation is mediated through spectatorship, political context, and media circulation [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It avoids trans theory in a direct sense because its focus is on lesbian identity rather than transgender embodiment, but it does engage film theory by showing how cinematic form can both reveal and obscure queer experience.

The evidence for In Between is more limited. The queer representation in Arab and Middle Eastern films article identifies it as one of three films in the case study, alongside Caramel and Circumstance [N4-F3]. It is described as set in Israel/Palestine and directed by Maysaloun Hamoud, but the provided excerpt does not give a detailed plot summary or analysis of trans identity [N4-F3]. This means that the close reading of In Between must be cautious and should not overstate what can be inferred from the evidence. The article does, however, emphasize that it is part of a comparative case study that examines how directors represent homosexuality in different social and cultural contexts [N4-F3]. This suggests that In Between is likely to be analyzed alongside the other films, but without more evidence, its specific trans-theoretical implications cannot be fully established here.

Overall, the three films in the evidence set differ in how they represent trans identity. Facing Mirrors is the most directly transgender-centered, with a trans protagonist and a narrative structure that frames trans identity as both personal and political [N3-F2]. Circumstance, by contrast, is more lesbian-centered and is used in the evidence as a cautionary example of how queer representation can be exoticized and stereotyped through cinematic form and reception [N3-F2]. In Between is a useful comparative case, but the available evidence is insufficient for a detailed close reading of its trans themes [N4-F3]. Across all three films, the evidence supports a film-theoretical approach that looks at dialogue, performance, mise-en-scène, narrative structure, and spectatorship [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It also supports a trans-theoretical approach that emphasizes embodiment, performativity, and the politics of visibility [N1-R5][N1-F1]. However, the evidence also shows that representation is often mediated by censorship, religion, and transnational media politics, which means that each film must be read in relation to its historical and institutional context [N3-F2][N4-F3].

Methodological and comparative synthesis across films and theories

This synthesis combines the theoretical foundations established in N8, the regional cinema context in N9, and the close reading of three films in N10 to identify common patterns, divergences, and the ways trans theory and film theory can be combined to interpret cinematic form. It also highlights limitations and implications for future research.

A major common pattern across the three films is the tension between visibility and marginalization. Trans theory emphasizes that visibility is historically contingent and often uneven [N1-R3], while the regional cinema context shows that Middle Eastern and North African films are shaped by censorship, religion, and uneven institutional support [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-F2]. In Facing Mirrors, this tension is especially visible: the film centers a transgender protagonist, yet its reception was uneven, with strong local reception in Iran but little mainstream Western coverage [N3-F2]. In Circumstance, the tension is mediated differently: the film was immediately picked up by Western media, but it was criticized by Iranian lesbians and feminists for being shallow and stereotypical [N3-F2]. In Between, the evidence is more limited, but the comparative case study framework suggests that trans representation is still shaped by the same regional and political conditions [N4-F3]. Taken together, these films show that trans visibility is not simply a matter of being on screen; it is shaped by local censorship, transnational media politics, and the ways films are received by different audiences.

A second common pattern is the use of coded or strategic representation. The queer representation in Arab and Middle Eastern films article notes that queer representations have been present since the 1930s, but always in coded forms [N4-F3]. This coding is especially important for understanding how filmmakers negotiate censorship and social stigma. In Facing Mirrors, the film’s narrative structure centers a trans protagonist whose identity is central to the story, yet the film’s production and reception are shaped by transnational media circuits and censorship [N3-F2]. In Circumstance, the coding is more aesthetic and narrative: the film uses a recognizable but ultimately problematic image of Iranian women’s sexuality, including American accents and anachronistic settings, which the evidence describes as a form of exoticization [N3-F2]. In In Between, the available evidence suggests that representation is still comparative and context-dependent, but it is positioned as part of a broader transnational queer cinema framework [N4-F3]. This pattern shows that trans theory helps identify how representation is not always explicit; it can be strategic, ambiguous, or even covert [N1-R4][N4-F3].

A third common pattern is the centrality of spectatorship and narrative form. Film theory in the evidence emphasizes spectatorship, narrative, and cinematic form as central areas of analysis [N5-R2][N5-R5]. The feminist film theory source notes that key paradigms include spectatorship and Narrative Cinema, with Mulvey’s work as a central reference [N5-R2]. The evidence on spectatorship and gender theory also argues that cinema can help struggles against norms and discrimination by showing how fantasy plays a role in spectatorship [N5-R3]. In the close reading of the three films, this means that each film must be read not only as a story about trans identity, but as a text that invites particular ways of watching and interpreting trans subjectivity. Facing Mirrors uses narrative structure and reception to position its trans protagonist as both local and global, while Circumstance uses mise-en-scène and narrative framing to create a recognizable but problematic image of lesbian experience [N3-F2]. In Between, by contrast, is presented as a comparative case study rather than a fully fleshed-out transgender film, which shows that the evidence is stronger for some films than for others [N4-F3]. This pattern supports a film-theoretical approach that treats cinematic form as a site of ideological and political mediation [N5-R2][N5-R3].

Despite these common patterns, there are important divergences across the films. The most direct divergence is between films centered on transgender identity and films centered on lesbian identity. Facing Mirrors is explicitly transgender-centered, with a pre-op transman protagonist and a narrative structure that frames trans identity as central to the story [N3-F2]. Circumstance, by contrast, is lesbian-centered and is used in the evidence as a cautionary case of how queer representation can be exoticized and stereotyped [N3-F2]. This divergence matters because it shows that trans theory and film theory can be used to analyze different kinds of queer representation, and that the two frameworks do not collapse into a single category. In other words, trans theory is especially useful for analyzing embodiment, performativity, and trans-specific subjectivity [N1-R5][N1-F1], while film theory is useful for analyzing spectatorship, narrative form, and cinematic structure [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also shows that In Between is part of a comparative case study, but its trans-theoretical implications are underdeveloped in the provided material [N4-F3]. This means that the comparative synthesis is partial and that future research should be more attentive to the limits of the evidence.

Another divergence is in how the films are mediated by regional and institutional context. Facing Mirrors is set in Iran and is produced by Iranian filmmakers, yet its reception is shaped by transnational media politics and censorship [N3-F2]. Circumstance is also set in Iran but is produced by an Iranian-American director and is immediately picked up by Western media, which the evidence describes as a result of the Orientalizing Western gaze [N3-F2]. In Between, by contrast, is set in Israel/Palestine and is presented as part of a broader transnational queer cinema framework [N4-F3]. These differences show that trans representation is not only a matter of content; it is also shaped by production context, distribution, and audience circuits. The regional cinema context in N9 emphasizes that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is historically embedded, institutionally uneven, and shaped by colonial and postcolonial forces [N2-R1][N2-R2]. This means that the same trans-theoretical claim can be interpreted differently depending on whether the film is produced within a conservative legal and religious context, a diasporic transnational context, or a comparative regional context [N3-F2][N4-F3].

A further divergence is in how the films engage or avoid trans theory and film theory claims. Facing Mirrors directly engages trans theory because it centers a transgender protagonist and uses narrative and reception to challenge dominant stereotypes [N3-F2]. Circumstance, by contrast, engages film theory more directly because its mise-en-scène, dialogue, and narrative form are used to examine how queer representation can be exoticized and stereotyped [N3-F2]. In Between is more limited in the evidence provided, so its engagement with trans theory and film theory cannot be fully assessed here [N4-F3]. This divergence suggests that trans theory and film theory are not interchangeable; they are complementary. Trans theory is especially useful for interpreting embodiment, performativity, and the politics of visibility [N1-R5][N1-F1], while film theory is especially useful for interpreting spectatorship, narrative form, and cinematic structure [N5-R2][N5-R3]. When combined, they can offer a more complete analysis of how transgender characters are represented on screen.

How trans theory and film theory can be combined to interpret cinematic form is therefore clear from the evidence. Trans theory helps identify the subject of representation: who the transgender character is, how their identity is performed, and what visibility means in their context [N1-R5][N1-R4]. Film theory helps identify the form of representation: how the narrative is structured, how the spectator is positioned, and how mise-en-scène, dialogue, and performance work together to produce meaning [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Together, they can be used to analyze not only whether a film represents transgender identity, but how it does so. In Facing Mirrors, this combination is useful because the film’s narrative structure and reception are both trans-theoretical and film-theoretical: the story is about trans embodiment and performativity, but it is also about how trans subjects are received by local and global audiences [N3-F2]. In Circumstance, the combination is useful because the film’s mise-en-scène and narrative form are used to examine how queer representation can be both visible and problematic [N3-F2]. In In Between, the combination is useful in principle, but the evidence is insufficient to make a detailed argument here [N4-F3].

Limitations, gaps, and implications for future research are therefore substantial. First, the evidence for In Between is incomplete, so any interpretation of that film must be cautious [N4-F3]. Second, the evidence for trans theory and film theory is uneven across the films: some films are more clearly transgender-centered, while others are more clearly lesbian-centered or comparative [N3-F2][N4-F3]. Third, the evidence is especially strong for the regional and institutional context, but it is less explicit about how trans theory should be applied to each film’s specific cinematic form [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-F2]. Fourth, the evidence suggests that future research should pay more attention to transnational media circuits, audience reception, and the ways in which trans representation is mediated by censorship, religion, and institutional power [N3-F2][N4-F3]. Finally, the evidence also suggests that future research should expand beyond the three films in the current set and include more direct trans-theoretical analyses of Middle Eastern and North African films, as well as more comparative work across trans, queer, and gendered representation [N8][N9][N10].

In conclusion, the methodological and comparative synthesis across films and theories shows that trans representation in Middle Eastern and North African cinema is best understood as a complex interplay of visibility, embodiment, spectatorship, narrative form, and regional context [N1-R5][N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. The three films in the evidence set illustrate both common patterns and important divergences, and they demonstrate that trans theory and film theory can be combined to interpret cinematic form in ways that are both historically sensitive and politically attentive [N3-F2][N4-F3]. At the same time, the evidence also highlights limitations that future research must address: insufficient evidence for some films, uneven theoretical engagement, and the need for more direct trans-theoretical analysis of cinematic form [N4-F3].

# Middle Eastern and North African Films with Transgender Themes

## Introduction

This paper explores Middle Eastern and North African films with transgender themes through a dual lens: trans theory and film theory. It begins by establishing the theoretical foundations that make transgender representation on screen meaningful, then situates those films within the broader regional cinema context of the Middle East and North Africa, and finally provides in-depth close readings of three films with transgender themes. The discussion is grounded in the evidence provided in the branch reports and is organized around the claim that transgender representation in regional cinema is best understood as a complex interplay of visibility, embodiment, spectatorship, narrative form, and regional context [N1-R5][N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. The paper concludes with a methodological synthesis that identifies common patterns, divergences, and limitations for future research.

## Theoretical Foundations for Transgender Representation in Film

Trans theory in the evidence is centered on gender performativity, trans embodiment, and visibility as the core concepts for analyzing transgender representation. Judith Butler’s theory of the performativity of gender is especially important here because the evidence explicitly states that drag performances and transgender identities reinforce Butler’s idea of gender as a performative act [N1-R5]. This is central to film analysis because it shifts the focus from identity as fixed or natural to identity as enacted, repeated, and contested on screen. Patricia Elliot is cited as an example of trans theorists who value transgressive transgender identities, which suggests that trans theory is often concerned with resisting normative categories and affirming marginalized identities [N1-R4]. This orientation is useful for evaluating how transgender characters are represented in film: they may be read as either subverting dominant norms or fitting into them, depending on the film’s context.

Trans embodiment is another central concept. The evidence from the trans/gender-variant filmmaking history article shows that trans and gender variant people have been making audiovisual media for a long time, and that trans filmmakers have begun to circulate amateur videos and digital media [N1-F1]. This historical claim challenges the idea that transgender representation is a recent or marginal phenomenon and suggests that trans embodiment and self-representation are deeply embedded in cinematic practice. The same source also critiques scholarship that reduces cross-dressing, drag, and trans representation to psychosexual metaphor or postmodern expression, arguing that such work can reiterate transphobic assumptions [N1-F1]. This critique matters because it warns against reading transgender bodies as symbolic or aesthetic objects rather than as embodied subjects with agency and history.

Visibility is the third key trans theory concept. The introduction to the special issue “Representing Trans” notes that trans representation has changed radically since the early 1990s, showing how visibility is historically contingent and uneven [N1-R3]. The evidence also states that trans persons are more represented in mainstream film and television, but that this increased visibility is still problematic because it can be uneven and often reinforced by dominant norms [N1-R2]. This matters for film theory because visibility is not simply about exposure; it is also about inclusion, exclusion, and the politics of representation. The trans/gender-variant filmmaking history article reinforces this point by showing that trans and gender variant people have been making audiovisual media for a long time, yet their work remains under-recognized or erased by mainstream media [N1-F1].

Film-theoretical concepts relevant to gendered spectatorship and narrative form are also central. The evidence on feminist film theory notes that key paradigms include spectatorship and Narrative Cinema, with Mulvey’s work as a central reference [N5-R2]. The same source describes feminist film theory as derived from feminist politics and feminist theory, influenced by second-wave feminism [N5-R5]. This is important because it shows that spectatorship is not merely passive viewing; it is about how audiences are positioned, how they interpret gendered content, and how gendered power relations are reproduced in the act of watching. The evidence on spectatorship and gender theory further argues that cinema can help struggles against norms and discrimination by showing how fantasy plays a role in spectatorship [N5-R3]. This is especially useful for analyzing transgender representation because it allows scholars to ask how transgender characters are framed, what fantasies or anxieties they trigger, and how those responses are mediated by the film’s form and narrative structure.

Narrative form is also a central film-theoretical concern. While the provided sources do not give a detailed taxonomy of narrative structures, they do situate spectatorship and narrative within a broader film-theoretical framework. The feminist film theory source mentions “Narrative Cinema” as a key paradigm, implying that narrative structure is a central object of analysis [N5-R2]. This is important because transgender representation often depends on how a story is told: whether the character’s trans identity is foregrounded, marginalized, or only implied; whether the narrative emphasizes agency, conflict, or conformity; and whether the film’s structure invites identification, resistance, or ambivalence from the spectator. The evidence on cross-dressing and transgender passing further supports this point by framing the transgender move as a site of agential potential in new Iranian cinema [N4-R2]. That concept is especially useful for film theory because it shifts the focus from identity as fixed to identity as performative and strategic within narrative.

Taken together, these theories can be used to critique or support representations of transgender characters. The evidence suggests that trans theory can be supportive when it foregrounds embodiment, performativity, and historical agency, as seen in the trans/gender-variant filmmaking history article [N1-F1]. It can also be critical when it exposes the limits of mainstream visibility, the risks of exoticization, and the ways trans bodies are often reduced to symbolic or aesthetic functions rather than treated as fully realized subjects [N1-R2][N1-F1]. Film theory, meanwhile, can support analysis by situating transgender representation within spectatorship, narrative form, and cinematic structure [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It can also critique representations by showing how films shape audience expectations, reinforce dominant gender norms, or open up new possibilities for reading trans identity. The intersection of trans theory and film theory therefore offers a powerful analytical tool: it can illuminate both how transgender characters are made visible and how those visibilities are shaped by cinematic form, narrative strategy, and the politics of spectatorship.

## Regional Cinema Context for Middle Eastern and North African Films

The regional cinema context for Middle Eastern and North African films is historically rooted but shaped by colonial, postcolonial, and contemporary institutional forces. The regional cinema guide notes that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is a broad term for film production across the region and that it includes reference resources, bibliographies, and aggregated information about the field [N2-R1]. Another source states that the course on Middle East/North Africa cinemas is designed to explore shared intra-regional cinematic trends and to situate these cinemas in the context of Third Cinema, which indicates that regional cinema is often understood as part of a broader anti-colonial or postcolonial cinematic tradition [N2-R2]. This framing is important because it suggests that Middle Eastern and North African cinema is not simply national cinema; it is also part of a transnational, politically inflected cinematic field shaped by historical struggle and representation.

Institutional context is also important. The regional cinema guide mentions that each chapter covers the history and major issues of film within a given area and provides bibliographies of leading films and directors [N2-R3]. The JSTOR source notes that there is a “plethora” of formal documented and inherited or experiential information about cinema in the Arab region, including reference books and encyclopedias [N2-R5]. These sources collectively indicate that regional film production has been documented over time, even as it has often been under-resourced or marginalized in mainstream global film histories. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article adds another layer: it states that Iranian filmmakers have been making films that tackle queer and trans subjects, but that such films are often ignored or excluded from dominant media discourses [N3-F2]. This suggests that institutional support, distribution, and visibility are uneven, and that regional cinema production is shaped by both local and global power structures.

Cultural and political factors shaping representation of gender and sexuality are central to this context. The queer and trans subjects in Iranian cinema article argues that Middle Eastern cinema has long been shaped by Orientalist fantasies and the Western gaze, which exoticize or misrepresent queer and trans subjects [N3-F2]. It also notes that the film Facing Mirrors, which features a female-to-male transgender protagonist, was widely received in Iran but received little mainstream Western coverage, highlighting the role of transnational media circuits and audience reception [N3-F2]. The article further compares this with Circumstance, which was immediately picked up by mainstream Western media but was criticized by Iranian lesbians and feminists for being shallow and stereotypical [N3-F2]. The article also emphasizes that the legal status of trans people in Iran is not simply liberal or conservative; it is complex, with legal acceptance coexisting with social invisibility and cultural marginalization [N3-F2].

## Methodological and Comparative Synthesis

### Common Patterns Across the Films

Across the three films, the evidence reveals several common patterns. First, visibility is uneven and historically contingent. Trans theory shows that visibility is not static; it changes over time and is shaped by social, political, and institutional conditions [N1-R3]. In Circumstance, the tension is mediated differently: the film was immediately picked up by Western media, but it was criticized by Iranian lesbians and feminists for being shallow and stereotypical [N3-F2]. In In Between, the evidence is more limited, but the comparative case study framework suggests that trans representation is still shaped by the same regional and political conditions [N4-F3].

Second, the films often use coded or strategic representation. The queer representation in Arab and Middle Eastern films article notes that queer representations have been present since the 1930s, but always in coded forms [N4-F3]. This coding is especially important for understanding how filmmakers negotiate censorship and social stigma. In Facing Mirrors, the film’s narrative structure centers a trans protagonist whose identity is central to the story, yet the film’s production and reception are shaped by transnational media circuits and censorship [N3-F2]. In Circumstance, the coding is more aesthetic and narrative: the film uses a recognizable but ultimately problematic image of Iranian women’s sexuality, including American accents and anachronistic settings, which the evidence describes as a form of exoticization [N3-F2]. In In Between, the available evidence suggests that representation is still comparative and context-dependent, but it is positioned as part of a broader transnational queer cinema framework [N4-F3]. This pattern shows that trans theory helps identify how representation is not always explicit; it can be strategic, ambiguous, or even covert [N1-R4][N4-F3].

Third, the films are centrally concerned with spectatorship and narrative form. Film theory emphasizes spectatorship, narrative, and cinematic form as central areas of analysis [N5-R2][N5-R5]. The feminist film theory source notes that key paradigms include spectatorship and Narrative Cinema, with Mulvey’s work as a central reference [N5-R2]. In the close reading of the three films, this means that each film must be read not only as a story about trans identity, but as a text that invites particular ways of watching and interpreting trans subjectivity. Facing Mirrors uses narrative structure and reception to position its trans protagonist as both local and global, while Circumstance uses mise-en-scène and narrative framing to create a recognizable but problematic image of lesbian experience [N3-F2]. In In Between, by contrast, the evidence is insufficient for a detailed argument, but the comparative framework suggests that cinematic form remains central to interpretation [N4-F3].

### Divergences Across the Films

Despite these common patterns, there are important divergences across the films. One major divergence is between films centered on transgender identity and films centered on lesbian identity. Facing Mirrors is explicitly transgender-centered, with a pre-op transman protagonist and a narrative structure that frames trans identity as central to the story [N3-F2]. Circumstance, by contrast, is lesbian-centered and is used in the evidence as a cautionary case of how queer representation can be exoticized and stereotyped [N3-F2]. This divergence matters because it shows that trans theory and film theory can be used to analyze different kinds of queer representation, and that the two frameworks do not collapse into a single category. In other words, trans theory is especially useful for analyzing embodiment, performativity, and trans-specific subjectivity [N1-R5][N1-F1], while film theory is especially useful for analyzing spectatorship, narrative form, and cinematic structure [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also shows that In Between is part of a comparative case study, but its trans-theoretical implications are underdeveloped in the provided material [N4-F3].
